blocks.text: You cannot fix what you have not measured. Before you drop a single duplicate row, fill a single missing value, or standardize a single inconsistent label, you need an honest answer to one question: how good is this data, really? Data quality assessment is the mandatory first step in every real cleaning workflow, and skipping it is one of the most common and costly mistakes people make when they first start working with messy datasets.

A proper assessment answers three things before any fixing begins. How bad is the problem, column by column. Where is it concentrated, is it spread evenly or is one source system responsible for most of it. And what kind of problem is it, missing data behaves nothing like a duplicate row, and a duplicate row behaves nothing like an inconsistently formatted label. Everything in this lesson is about getting to those answers quickly, using tools you already have in pandas.
1. The Six Dimensions of Data Quality

Data quality is not a single yes or no property of a dataset. It is commonly broken down into six dimensions, each capturing a different way data can go wrong, and each needing a different kind of check to detect. Knowing these six by name is what turns a vague feeling that 'this data looks messy' into a concrete, checkable list.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Dimension","Definition","Concrete Example"],"rows":[["Completeness","Are the values that should be present actually present, or are they missing","A customer record with no phone number and no email on file, so there is no way to reach them at all"],["Accuracy","Are the values correct and true to reality, not just present and reasonably formatted","A customer's recorded age is 34 but they are actually 41. The value exists and looks perfectly normal, it is simply wrong"],["Consistency","Does the same fact appear the same way everywhere it is recorded","One system logs a customer's state as NY, a second logs it as New York, a third logs it as ny"],["Validity","Does a value conform to the expected format, range, or type for that field","An age column containing negative numbers or a value like 200, or an email field with no @ symbol in it"],["Uniqueness","Are there duplicate records that should logically be a single entity","The same customer appears three times because they signed up once through the app, once through the website, and once through a support call"],["Timeliness","Is the data current enough to still be useful for the decision it will be used for","A customer's address on file is four years old and they have since moved twice"]]}

blocks.text: These six overlap in practice more than the clean definitions suggest. A value can be perfectly valid while still being inaccurate, and that distinction matters enough to call out on its own.

blocks.title: Validity is not the same thing as accuracy
blocks.content: An age of 34 is a valid integer inside a plausible human range, so a validity check will happily let it through. If the person is actually 41, that value is still wrong, it is just wrong in a way that looks fine on the surface. Accuracy usually requires comparing against some external source of truth, which is why most automated tooling checks validity as a practical, checkable stand in for accuracy rather than accuracy itself.

blocks.text: 2. A Practical Assessment Workflow in Pandas

Each of the six dimensions maps to a small, specific set of pandas calls. None of them are complicated on their own, the value is in running all of them, in order, on every new dataset before writing a single line of cleaning code.
2.1 Checking Completeness

A raw missing count does not mean much on its own, a column with 40 missing values could be a disaster in a 100 row dataset or a non issue in a 500,000 row dataset. Turning the count into a percentage fixes that.

A column sitting at 2 percent missing and a column sitting at 60 percent missing call for completely different responses, and this single line is what tells you which situation you are actually in before you decide anything.
2.2 Checking Validity

dtypes tells you what type pandas believes each column holds, which is the first sanity check, an age column stored as an object instead of a number is already a red flag. describe surfaces the numeric range of every column in one call, and that range is where the loudest validity problems tend to show up.

An age column with a minimum of negative 3 and a maximum of 200 is immediately suspect, since no real person has either of those ages. Neither value is missing, neither is technically malformed as a number, but both are outside the range that makes sense for what the column represents, which is exactly what a validity check is looking for.
2.3 Checking Uniqueness
duplicated flags every row that is an exact repeat of a row seen earlier, and summing that boolean result gives you a single count of exact duplicate rows in the dataset.

The subset argument matters in practice more than the plain call does. Two rows rarely match on every single column, but they very often share the same logical key, the same customer_id or the same order_id, while differing slightly in a timestamp or a field that got re entered. Checking duplication on the key you actually care about surfaces far more real duplicates than checking for exact whole row matches.
2.4 Checking Consistency

value_counts on a categorical column lists every distinct label pandas sees, sorted from most to least frequent, and it is usually the fastest way to spot inconsistent labeling for the same underlying value.

code.content:
print(df["state"].value_counts())
# NY          412
# New York     88
# ny           15
# Ny            4

blocks.text: Nothing in pandas knows that NY, New York, ny, and Ny all refer to the same state, that requires a human, or a mapping a human writes, to decide. What value_counts gives you is the first and most important step, a clear, sorted list of every variant actually present in the column, so the inconsistency is visible instead of hidden inside a column that looks fine at a glance.
2.5 Accuracy and Timeliness Need Outside Context

Unlike the previous four, accuracy and timeliness usually cannot be checked from the dataset alone. Accuracy needs comparison against a trusted external source, a government ID database, a verified purchase record, something outside the DataFrame you are looking at. Timeliness needs an expected freshness window that depends entirely on what the data is used for, a stock price is stale after a few seconds while a home address is fine for months. When a last updated timestamp exists, checking it against the current date is the closest thing to an automatic timeliness check available.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

days_old = (pd.Timestamp.now() - df["last_updated"]).dt.days
print((days_old > 365).sum())  # rows not touched in over a year

blocks.text: 3. Worked Example: Computing a Data Quality Score
Putting numbers on the previous section makes it concrete. Take a small ten row customer dataset with a handful of realistic problems planted in it.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

data = {
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 8, 10],
    "age":         [34, None, 41, -5, 29, 200, 51, None, 8, 33],
    "email":       ["a@x.com", "b@x.com", None, "d@x.com", "e@x.com",
                    "f@x.com", "g@x.com", "h@x.com", "h@x.com", "j@x.com"],
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

blocks.text: customer_id 8 appears twice, age has two missing values plus two implausible ones (negative 5 and 200), and email has one missing value plus one repeated address. Scoring each dimension separately shows exactly how each problem gets counted.

code.content:
total_cells = df.size
missing_cells = df.isnull().sum().sum()
completeness_pct = (1 - missing_cells / total_cells) * 100
# 3 missing out of 30 total cells -> (1 - 3/30) * 100 = 90.0

valid_ages = df["age"].between(0, 120)
validity_pct = valid_ages.sum() / df["age"].notna().sum() * 100
# 6 valid ages out of 8 non null ages -> 6/8 * 100 = 75.0

uniqueness_pct = df["customer_id"].nunique() / len(df) * 100
# 9 unique ids out of 10 rows -> 9/10 * 100 = 90.0

quality_score = (completeness_pct + validity_pct + uniqueness_pct) / 3
# (90.0 + 75.0 + 90.0) / 3 = 85.0

print(f"Completeness: {completeness_pct:.1f}%")
print(f"Validity:     {validity_pct:.1f}%")
print(f"Uniqueness:   {uniqueness_pct:.1f}%")
print(f"Overall data quality score: {quality_score:.1f}%")

blocks.text: Each percentage traces back to a specific, countable problem: three missing cells, two out of range ages, one duplicate customer id. Nothing here is subjective, the whole point of the exercise is turning 'this data seems kind of messy' into three numbers you can compare against the next dataset, or track over time as a pipeline runs.

blocks.title: A quality score is a compass, not a verdict
blocks.content: There is no universal formula for combining the six dimensions into one number, and a plain average is a simplification made for this example. In practice you weight the dimensions that matter most for how the data will actually be used. If a model only ever reads the age column, a validity problem there deserves far more weight than a missing email address, even though a plain average would treat them equally.

blocks.text: 4. The Data Profiling Report

A data profiling report is the standard deliverable that comes out of an assessment, produced before any cleaning code is written. At minimum it lists, per column, the type, the missing percentage, the number of unique values, the observed range, and any anomalies the checks above turned up.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Column","Type","Missing %","Unique Values","Min / Max","Flags"],"rows":[["customer_id","int64","0%","9","1 to 10","1 duplicate id (8 appears twice)"],["age","float64","20%","8","-5 to 200","2 out-of-range values (-5 and 200)"],["email","object","10%","8","n/a","1 duplicate value (h@x.com used twice)"]]}

blocks.text: This is exactly the kind of one page summary that should exist before a single line of cleaning code gets written. Once it exists, every decision that follows, what to drop, what to fill, what to standardize, is grounded in an actual measurement instead of a guess made while staring at a few random rows.
5. Why Skipping This Step Is a Costly Mistake

The most common shortcut is jumping straight to fixing missing values, usually with something like filling every numeric column with its mean, without ever running isnull().mean() first. If a column turns out to be 80 percent missing, filling it does not rescue useful data, it manufactures data that was never there, and the column probably should have been dropped entirely instead.

The deeper cost is missing the reason the data is missing in the first place. Suppose a years_at_company field is missing only for contractors, never for full time employees. That pattern is a real signal about how the data was collected, not random noise, and filling it with the median silently erases that signal from the dataset. An assessment that checks missingness against other columns catches this. Jumping straight to fillna does not, because nothing about fillna asks why a value is absent.

There is also an effort problem. Real datasets rarely have quality issues spread evenly across every column, the damage is usually concentrated in one or two columns, or traceable back to a single source system that feeds the pipeline. Without profiling first, it is easy to spend a week building careful cleaning logic for a column with a minor issue while a genuinely broken column sits untouched because nobody looked at it closely enough to notice.

blocks.title: A pattern worth remembering
blocks.content: A team spends days writing sophisticated imputation logic for a column that turns out, on inspection, to be 95 percent missing and should simply have been dropped. A single line, df.isnull().mean(), would have caught this in seconds and saved the entire effort. This is the concrete cost of skipping assessment, not a hypothetical one.

blocks.text: 6. Automated Profiling Tools

Everything covered above can also be generated automatically. Libraries like ydata-profiling, formerly known as pandas-profiling, take a DataFrame and produce a full HTML report covering missing values, types, distributions, correlations, and flagged warnings in one call. It is worth knowing this category of tool exists, especially for a first look at a new dataset with many columns, though it does not replace understanding what each check above is actually doing.

code.content:
from ydata_profiling import ProfileReport

profile = ProfileReport(df, title="Dataset Quality Report")
profile.to_file("report.html")

blocks.text: Production pipelines still tend to rely on the small, explicit, targeted checks from the previous sections rather than a full HTML report, since those checks are easy to automate, log, and alert on. Treat automated profiling tools as a fast way to get oriented on an unfamiliar dataset, not as a replacement for knowing what completeness, validity, and uniqueness actually mean.
7. Recap: What a Proper Assessment Produces

items: A per column missing percentage, not just a raw count, so you know how bad each gap actually is relative to the size of the dataset.
A validity check against expected ranges and types, catching values like negative ages or a 200 year old customer before they ever reach a model.
A duplicate count, both exact row duplicates and duplicates on a logical key like customer_id, since real duplicates rarely match on every single column.
A pass over categorical columns using value_counts to catch inconsistent labeling, like NY, New York, and ny all representing the same value.
A documented sense of how fresh the data is relative to when and how it will actually be used.
A single profiling report, or at minimum a short summary table, that the whole team can reference before any cleaning code gets written.

blocks.text: Only once this picture exists do the lessons that follow in this module, on handling missing values, removing duplicate records, and fixing inconsistent data, actually make sense. Assessment is what tells you exactly which of them to reach for, and exactly where.
